items.question: Why do you see understanding the inner workings of neural networks as critical to Goodfire’s mission?
items.object: AI interpretability and Goodfire’s purpose
items.answer: So Goodfire is an AI interpretability research company really trying to answer the question of what's actually going on inside the mind of a neural net. The ultimate goal and the reason why we started everything was we just see neural networks going into more and more mission critical contexts, and I think it's going to be enormously transformative for society. In order to do so, you want to build it safely, powerfully, reliably, and I think it's going to be critical to be able to understand, edit, and debug AI models in order to do that. That's what we're enabling for the very first time. It's unlocking the black box of a neural network such that you can intentionally design it rather than just grow it from data.
quotes: So Goodfire is an AI interpretability research company really trying to answer the question of, you know, what's actually going on inside the mind of a neural net.

The ultimate goal and the reason why we started everything was we just see neural networks going into more and more mission critical contexts, and I think it's going to be enormously transformative for society.
In order to do so, you want to build it safely, powerfully, reliably, and I think it's going to be critical to be able to understand, edit, and debug AI models in order to do that.
That's what we're enabling for the very first time. It's unlocking the black box of a neural network such that you can intentionally design it rather than just grow it from data.

items.question: How do you think looking inside neural networks could help you assess whether AI models are trustworthy in mission-critical applications?
items.object: Interpretability as a way to assess trust in AI models
items.answer: So I guess maybe thinking about what would happen if we were to just deploy AI models as black boxes in perpetuity. The black box way to do this would be—and I'm kind of assuming that we're playing this forward a few years and we want AI in charge of really mission critical applications, like maybe being in charge of our power grid or making big investment decisions, maybe even for a seed investment at Sequoia or a really large million dollar investment decision. I think the black box way to make sure that the AI is performing appropriately is you take a look at evals and you run a bunch of evaluations to make sure that it's behaving appropriately in test sets, and then you look at its track record and see if it's reliable enough to perform across a wide variety of things. I think the question then is, why not take all of this additional signal that you get from looking inside a neural network and trying to play forward how it's going to behave in a much wider, broader set of situations? Why not look inside and actually get a bunch more reliability, certainty about how it's thinking, how it's approaching the problem? I think you're just leaving a bunch on the table if you're not looking for all the signal that you can get. The way that I think about this is, I don't know, when you're manufacturing a new drug, you can do the black box way of just seeing how humans respond to the drug in a clinical trial. Whereas you could also look inside and look at biochemically how the drug is processed or drug interactions at the molecular or cellular level. I just feel like there's so much to be learned when you actually look inside and deeply understand something.

items.question: How do you assess the possibility of deeply understanding a neural network through mechanistic interpretability?
items.object: The feasibility and importance of mechanistic interpretability
items.answer: Well, I'm very biased, but I think it's very possible. A lot of the people in mechanistic interpretability come from backgrounds in computational neuroscience or cognitive science, and those people, when you're actually looking inside the brain, spend so much time trying to understand what a single neuron does or just getting any signal whatsoever. In the field of mechanistic interpretability, you have perfect access to the neurons, the parameters, the weights, the attention patterns of a neural network. So you're coming in with a huge advantage; at least you get all of the data that you need. So then the real question is, how can we make progress? How can we try to understand and seek to understand all of it? I think we just got to try. I think it's deeply necessary and critical for the future.

items.question: Why do you think understanding the inner workings of neural networks is critical to AI’s future?
items.object: The importance of understanding neural networks for intentionally designing AI
items.answer: Yeah, I think it's going to be critical for the future just given how transformative I think AI is going to be. I think AI is going to be everywhere, running mission critical parts of our society. We can get really far just by treating AI as a black box, but I don't think we can truly be able to intentionally design AI as the new generation of software without white box techniques. Maybe one example I think about is, in the early 17th century, you invented the steam engine and were able to increase the size of the boiler and increase the amount of pressure going in, and it scaled reasonably well. But steam engines also blew up. We didn't understand thermodynamics at that time. So we didn't actually know at what point the ideal size of the boiler or the ideal pressure, the ideal way to construct a steam engine. After we invented thermodynamics, things started becoming a lot safer, a lot more reliable, and huge innovations happened afterwards. But already the steam engine kicked off the industrial revolution. So even just by treating it as a black box, you get a really long way.

items.question: How do you think understanding neural networks could help us understand human thought?
items.object: The potential for understanding neural networks to illuminate human thought
items.answer: I think so. But that's a big claim, I think. We were just having an interesting conversation last night. We had a dinner together about, do we think in language? Do you think in concepts or something else entirely? I'm a person that doesn't really think in language. I think much more conceptually, maybe in the latent space of models. Whereas our head of product, Myra, said that she basically is totally faithful to her own chain of thought, speaks in language, and she basically just thinks sequentially with a really strong internal monologue. So maybe some of these insights that we get will translate to humans and our own psychology. And I think that's the hope. The more that we can understand about AI, hopefully the more that we can understand about ourselves.

items.question: How do you understand the idea of universality in neural networks?
items.object: Universality in neural networks
items.answer: There's this concept of universality where among totally different neural networks, similar kinds of circuits or thought patterns tend to emerge between all these neural networks. Even in vision models, we found very similar kinds of circuits to our own visual cortex. I think there's this idea of universality where maybe intelligence is just this thing that you gradient descent to, and that's how our brains found intelligence and that's how artificial minds would find intelligence as well. There's some truth to intelligence.

items.question: How do you think interpretability could change the way you grow and shape neural networks?
items.object: AI interpretability as a way to intentionally shape neural networks
items.answer: So maybe one metaphor that we like and think about is, right now you just kind of grow AI from a seed and then it grows like a giant tree and it grows all wild and crazy. Right now we don't really know a lot of the things that it's growing into, and all sorts of interesting and weird stuff can happen with the really large neural net. But if everything goes right with interpretability, we'll know how every single piece of training data affects the cognition that the model develops, the units of computation that it uses. I almost think of it more as bonsai, where you want to intentionally design and shape and grow the neural network, still in an unsupervised, AI driven approach. We're not going to hand prune every single weight of a neural network, but I think we'll gain the ability during every single piece of the training, post-training process to intentionally shape an AI model such that it serves humanity and does what we want.

items.question: How do you think about the relationship between shaping a neural network’s behavior and directly editing it?
items.object: Shaping and directly editing neural networks through interpretability
items.answer: I think in interpretability as a field, there's still a lot to figure out, and so it's still pretty new. But I think in bonsai you also prune a lot of branches and you prune a lot of the areas that you don't want to grow, such that you can shape the overall tree to grow in the pattern that you want. I think the eventual system that we hope to build, you can ask questions of the model like, why did you come up with this response, and get a faithful explanation, while also being able to make direct surgical interventions in the mind of the model such that we can remove harmful behavior, enhance good behavior. It still remains to be seen whether it's just a direct weights modification or some other kind of shaping function that is most effective.

items.question: How do you interpret the implications of Owen Evans’s group’s emergent misalignment study for steering AI models through fine-tuning?
items.object: Model steering through fine-tuning and Owen Evans’s group’s emergent misalignment study
items.answer: Fundamentally, these are black box things. All sorts of weird things can happen when you fine-tune a model, for example, or prompt a model and take it out of distribution, and it can say all sorts of crazy stuff. The paper that's most interesting about this recently is this emergent misalignment study. Owen Evans's group: if you fine-tune a model on just insecure code, so it's bad code that has all sorts of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, it'll then start doing all sorts of insane things, like wanting to enslave humanity or praising Hitler and other dictators. And it's a really surprising result because it's just insecure code. It kind of shows that maybe what you're doing with fine-tuning is you're telling the model, hey, do more of this, less of this, and almost enhancing the circuits that you want more of, but you can also have all sorts of unintended consequences like this that show up. And these circuits are still really alien cognition. There's some parallels to humanity, but we really don't understand how these networks think, and they're not like human thinking. So if you enhance the bad code snippets, it's also fundamentally linked to maybe all sorts of other undesirable behaviors and properties.

items.answer: I think it's just a function of how they're trained, and it's really hard to anticipate in advance. I don't know. I feel like it might just be me, but Claude 4 Opus 2 is enormously sycophantic. I'll kind of nudge it in one direction and it'll just agree with me wholeheartedly, and then nudge it in the other direction, pose a counterexample, and it'll just be like, yes, I was totally wrong before. Nothing I said earlier was correct. I just think it's really hard. It kind of goes back to the witchcraft almost of training an AI model today, where you're throwing training data into the model and whispering the incantation of gradient descent and then trying to get what you want out of it, and something pops out and then it really cares about animals. items.question: Why do you see the Circuits thread as such an important starting point for mechanistic interpretability?
items.object: The Circuits thread and its role in mechanistic interpretability
items.answer: In my mind, this was almost the start of the field of mechanistic interpretability. It posited three things. One is there are features in neural networks, which are directions in latent space that represent concepts that the model uses to generate its response. Circuits are features that fire together to create higher order concepts. The example they lay out is you have a car window detector, then a car body detector, then a car wheel detector, and that's a car circuit. Universality is the third tenet: similar circuits evolve in different neural networks. That really kicked off a lot of interesting research and results, and the feature circuits paradigm.

items.question: Why do you regard sparse autoencoders as such a significant advance in understanding superposition in neural networks?
items.object: Superposition and sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability
items.answer: One of the other really key things to have happened was understanding and mostly resolving superposition. Superposition is this idea that each neuron is responsible for encoding multiple concepts and there are more concepts than dimensions in a neural network. I think about a neural network as a giant compression algorithm. You're compressing the entirety of the internet into a relatively small number of parameters. So that means every single neuron needs to encode, or at least every single layer of the model needs to encode, more concepts than it has dimensions. There's this concept of superposition where you have concepts represented as near orthogonal directions in latent space, such that you can represent all of these concepts in a model's latent space. To resolve this, you have to almost untangle and unscramble a neuron such that it's responsible for one clean, interpretable concept. A group at Apollo Research, led by Lee Sharkey, who's now at Goodfire, first pioneered sparse autoencoders for language models, and Anthropic also really popularized this with their big paper, Towards Monosemanticity, and then right afterwards, Scaling Monosemanticity, showing that you can essentially unscramble these neurons into higher order concepts reliably and at scale with arbitrarily large neural networks. I think that was a really big moment for interpretability where you can now, in a totally unsupervised way, unscramble neurons of a neural network to understand them and get clean concepts. The concepts aren't totally clean yet. You can't edit them super well. There's all sorts of problems with this, but it's almost a really big step forward for the field such that we can do this in an unsupervised way, and the techniques in interpretability scale, which is really important.

items.answer: So I think it means it was real. Neurons are responsible for encoding multiple concepts, such that once you unscramble them then you can do really interesting things with a clean neuron. The way that we do this is using an interpreter model trained on the activations of a base model, and now you have all sorts of neurons in the interpreter model that represent theoretically clean sparse concepts. The original model still has this characteristic of superposition.

items.question: Why do you think interpretability techniques can keep pace as AI models become more intelligent?
items.object: Auto interpretability and the scalability of AI interpretability techniques
items.answer: I think the techniques that we've developed work on toy models all the way up to big networks that are more capable and more intelligent and better, and I think the techniques also scale effectively with model intelligence. One part of our pipeline is that for every single latent concept in our interpreter model, we get another language model to reason about what that concept actually represents in the base model. So this is a concept called auto interpretability, which Nick Cammarata, who's at Goodfire now, invented this technique at OpenAI, pioneered. This technique, because it's a language model reasoning about what a neuron represents, scales with the quality of the language model, so it actually gets better. Because we use AI in order to understand AI, the better our models, these analysis agents, are at interpreting what's actually going on, the better we're able to understand them.

items.question: Why are you excited about interpreting Arc Institute’s EVO 2 DNA foundation model?
items.object: Interpreting Arc Institute’s EVO 2 DNA foundation model
items.answer: We worked with Arc Institute to understand and interpret EVO 2, which is their DNA foundation model. It's a sequence-to-sequence model. It takes in a sequence of nucleotides and predicts the next nucleotide in a sequence. Our theory is this is a narrowly superhuman model. We really like to work on narrowly superhuman models because it can teach us something about the world that humans don't really know. The idea is this model is representing an enormous amount about the biological world in order to generate and properly model the next nucleotide in a sequence. What we did was we sought to understand what it actually knows such that it can model the world so effectively. We trained sparse autoencoders on the activations of this model, extracted all sorts of features that were related to concepts that the model should know, normal biological concepts that we have really strong ground truth annotations for. These are tRNAs, RNAs, start coding sequences, all sorts of biological concepts that we have ground truth annotations for, associated with this model. Then the question is, okay, now we have all of these other features of the model that we've extracted. What do they mean? What are they? They might just be ways that the model is computing and thinking, or they could represent novel biological concepts that the model's using to generate the next nucleotide in a sequence.

items.question: What do you hope unsupervised AI techniques can reveal about DNA?

items.answer: I think hopefully using unsupervised AI techniques we can better understand what all these portions of the DNA are actually doing. Maybe we can discover the idea of junk DNA faster, or understand that DNA is not junk DNA faster, and just discover totally novel things that genes are doing and expressing within us.

items.question: How do you assess Goodfire’s current ability to control and edit models through interpretability?
items.object: Goodfire’s ability to control and edit models through interpretability
items.answer: We've done most of our editing work on language models and image models. Our most recent release was Paint with Ember. Ember is our foundational infrastructure for interpretability. What we were able to do with this image model demo was targeted, precise control over an image model by painting. We could extract latent concepts like a dragon or dragon wings or an ocean or a pyramid, and then take these concepts and directly intervene on the portion of a canvas that we want to intervene on. You can paint a dragon with wings and then add a crowd in the corner and add a pyramid. It's a really fun demo that's a joy to play with. It's out right now; anybody can play with it. It's paint.goodfire.ai. We're able to reasonably intervene in certain situations on a model's latents and steer the model to do what we want. But we haven't quite cracked the idea of direct precision surgical edits that create a new model that you want to use and doesn't have any unintended side effects. That's still something that we're pushing on and trying to figure out.

items.question: How broadly do you see interpretability shaping the future of AI?
items.object: Interpretability’s future role in AI
items.answer: I think there are many places where the field is going to go. Interpretability is almost such a general term that, again, I'm biased, but I think it's just governing and underlying all aspects of AI. Anytime you prefer to take a white box approach to doing something versus a black box approach, interpretability can probably help in the future.

items.question: How do you see interpretability changing the AI development process?
items.object: Interpretability’s role in AI development
items.answer: Maybe you want to understand whether the training data is surprising to the model before putting it into the model, because then it can have the most impact on training. Just in every single part of the AI development stack, I think interpretability will help and change the way that we do things.

Auditing: how do you take a model, understand what's going on, find problematic behavior and good behavior, hopefully get rid of the bad behavior and enhance the good behavior? As AI gets deployed in more and more mission critical contexts, that becomes more important.

items.question: What interests you about comparing different checkpoints of an AI model?

items.answer: We're interested in model diffing. When you have two checkpoints of a model, how do they differ from each other and what's changed? The recent GPT-4o was enormously sycophantic for a period of time, just telling the user that they're doing great.

items.question: How do you assess the team you’ve assembled at Goodfire to tackle interpretability?
items.object: Goodfire’s interpretability team
items.answer: I think we have a really fantastic team, and that's what we've been spending a lot of our time on the last year, assembling a team of world-class interpretability experts that really have a shot of cracking this problem. It starts with my co-founders. I had worked with Dan Balsam, our CTO, for many years at my previous company. Our chief scientist Tom founded the interpretability team at Google DeepMind way back in the day. We've assembled many of the early folks in the field. Tom, Nick Cammarata, who's working very closely with Chris Olah, who's generally considered the founder of the field of mechanistic interpretability. Nick was on all of the original Circuits papers and helped build everything out at OpenAI. Lee Sharkey, who pioneered sparse autoencoders on language models, is now working on some really interesting work in weight based interpretability. Most interpretability techniques that have been deployed into applications are in concept space and activation space, and he and his group are working on weight space interpretability techniques. We've also pulled in scientists, senior scientists from other fields who care a lot about interpretability and have realized that this is one of the most important problems that we can work on. Owen Lewis, who was a senior staff research scientist at Google working on coding agents, came over and is now leading a couple directions here for us.

items.question: Why do you think an independent mechanistic interpretability company offers something valuable alongside research teams inside foundation model labs?
items.object: Independent mechanistic interpretability research companies
items.answer: I think we can just take a really different approach if we're independent. The benefit of being independent is we can think independently, push things forward independently, and also get a broader view of the ecosystem. Usually if you're within a lab, you're doing interpretability work on your own models and pushing forward the field in that way, and you can make incredible progress that way. But I really do think that a unique third party perspective is deeply necessary in the field. Given the team that we've assembled, a lot of those folks agree with that and that's why they've joined. It also gives us an ability to work with lots of interesting partners across different domains, and we can unify those insights across all these different domains that teach us more about the inner workings of neural networks more broadly. We work across modalities like genomics models, exomic models, image, video, language, and also across model architectures, and all that just helps.
